pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; What Is Wind? (CONCEPTUAL, 0.06): wind is moving air; it can be a gentle breeze or a strong gale; wind can move things — leaves, kites, flags — and even push people.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes' — describing windy weather). The cause of wind (uneven heating) is deferred to 7-9 'What Causes Wind'. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS2-1 (VERIFIED verbatim) names wind among weather conditions (DCI ESS2.D). Keep it to 'wind is moving air' + strength, observed by its EFFECTS — mechanism is later.
• Operational details — The core idea is that wind is AIR that is MOVING — invisible itself, known by what it does (things move, flags flap, you feel it push). The second idea is strength as a spectrum: breeze → gale. At this age, do NOT explain what makes wind blow (uneven heating/rising air is the 7-9 topic this feeds); keep to observing and describing. Confront the intuitive gap that 'air is nothing' — wind proves air is real 'stuff' that can push. Prerequisite: none; feeds What Causes Wind (7-9) and Using Weather Instruments (anemometer/wind vane). Evidence: define wind as moving air; distinguish breeze vs strong wind; give examples of what wind moves.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child defines wind as moving air, tells a gentle breeze from a strong wind, and gives examples of things wind can move or push — recognising wind by its effects, with no requirement to explain what causes it.
bestPractices: Make wind's invisibility concrete: we can't see air, but we see and feel what it DOES (leaves swirl, flag snaps, hair blows, it pushes you) — wind is evidence that air is real 'stuff'.
Build strength as a spectrum (breeze → wind → gale) with matching effects (leaves flutter → branches sway → hard to walk), rather than just 'windy/not windy'.
Use first-hand experience — blow on a hand, wave a fan, take a windy-day walk, fly a streamer — before any screen, so the concept is embodied.
Keep cause OUT at this age: resist 'wind is made by trees waving' (reversed cause) or 'the sky/clouds make wind'; the uneven-heating explanation is the 7-9 topic.
Link to safety and daily life gently (strong wind can knock things over, makes kites fly) without tipping into the separate storm-safety content.
Distinguish wind (moving air outdoors) from a fan/breath (moving air we make) — same idea, different source.
keyRepresentations: A wind-strength slider from breeze to gale with a scene that responds (leaves → branches → whole tree), an informal Beaufort-style scale for young children.
Wind socks / flags / streamers whose angle shows wind strength and direction — the classic 'see the invisible' device.
Effect cards: things wind moves (kite, leaves, flag, hat, washing) vs things it can't easily move (heavy rock).
A hand feeling a fan/blow — embodied 'air is real and can push'.
commonMisconceptions: 'Wind is made by trees waving' (or fans/clouds) — reversed cause: the moving air makes the trees wave, not the other way round.
'Air is nothing / empty' — wind demonstrates air is real matter that can push objects and be felt.
'Wind blows because the weather is angry / on purpose' — animistic framing; keep it to observation, defer real cause.
'Windy always means cold' — wind can be warm or cold; strength and temperature are separate.
'You can see the wind' — we see its EFFECTS and things it carries, not the moving air itself.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, build the idea that wind is moving air — invisible itself, but known by what it does (leaves swirl, flags snap, hair blows, it pushes you) — and that wind has a strength spectrum from gentle breeze to strong gale. Confront the intuition that 'air is nothing' by showing air is real stuff that can push. Keep the CAUSE of wind (uneven heating/rising air) out at this age; that is a later 7–9 topic. Ground learning in first-hand experience (blowing, fanning, a windy-day walk) before any screen model.

activities.title: Make your own wind
feedback: If a learner thinks air is 'nothing', have them blow on their hand: 'You just felt the air push — so air is real stuff, even though we can't see it.'
If a learner thinks wind must come from one place like the sky, show it can be made from any direction by fanning: 'Wind is air moving from place to place, not pouring out of one spot.'
Distinguish gently: 'A fan and your breath are moving air YOU make; outdoor wind is moving air outdoors — same idea, different source.'
activities.rationale: First-hand, embodied experience of moving air makes 'air is real and can push' concrete before any screen model and directly addresses the 'air is nothing' and 'wind comes from one fixed source' misconceptions. Leading with this hands-on work matches the stated pedagogy of first-hand experience before any on-screen model.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
learnerActions: Blow on the back of your own hand and feel the push.
Wave a hand or a fan at your face and feel the moving air.
Wave a streamer or strip of paper and watch it flutter in the air you move.
Talk about where outdoor wind is the same idea (moving air) but comes from outside rather than from you.
Indoors with the windows shut, work out how you could still make a little wind yourself (blow, fan, wave) — showing wind is just air moving, not something from a single fixed source.
activities.intendedInsight: Air is real stuff you can feel, and wind is simply air that is moving. You can make moving air yourself with your breath or a fan — the same idea as outdoor wind, just a different source.

activities.title: Crank the wind from breeze to gale
feedback: When a learner says 'but I can't see any wind', affirm it: 'Right — we never see the air. We see what it DOES: the leaves move, the flag snaps, the hat rolls away.'
If a learner expects everything to move equally, point to the rock: 'A gentle breeze moves a leaf but not a heavy rock. How strong did you have to make it before the branches moved?'
Connect to their body: 'When you crank it to a gale the character leans in to walk — have you ever felt the wind push you like that?'
activities.rationale: Used after the first-hand experience, a responsive scene the child controls lets them vary strength and watch what each level can and cannot move, building both 'wind is moving air (seen through effects)' and the breeze–gale spectrum together. The draggable 'can it move this?' test and the leaning windsock are concrete ways to make the invisible readable. This is one effective model, not the only way, and it supports rather than replaces feeling real wind.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
learnerActions: Use a wind-strength control (e.g. a slider or dial) that goes from gentle breeze up to strong gale, coupled to an outdoor scene that responds live.
Nudge the strength up a little and watch a few leaves stir and a flag ripple — name this a breeze.
Push the strength higher and watch branches sway, a kite lift and pull on its string, and hair stream sideways.
Push to the top and watch the whole tree bend, a hat tumble off and roll away, and a character lean hard into the gust to keep walking — name this a gale.
Drag objects into the scene and test 'can the wind move this?' — compare a leaf (blows away) with a heavy rock (stays put).
Read a windsock or flag whose angle leans further as the strength increases, showing the invisible wind's strength and direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is moving air: you never see the air itself, only what it does. By changing the strength yourself in the model, you see wind as moving air of varying strength — a spectrum from breeze to gale — recognised by its effects, and you can link this to how real wind has felt on your body.

activities.title: Which way does the cause go? (trees and wind)
feedback: Correct answer: 'It's the other way round. Wind is moving air. The moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees aren't making the wind. We can't see the air itself, but we can see what it does.'
If a learner names the moving object as the cause, flip it: show a still day (nothing waves), then a fan making a still branch wave — the air moves the object, not the other way round.
Keep the real cause of wind aside: 'We're not working out what makes the wind blow today — just that the wind moves the trees, not the trees making the wind.'
activities.rationale: Reversed causality ('trees waving make the wind') is a documented young-learner misconception; directly contrasting a windless scene with a fan moving a still object makes the direction of cause visible without introducing the deferred uneven-heating mechanism.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
learnerActions: Look at or imagine a windy day with tree branches waving about.
Consider a claim: 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Decide whether it is right and explain why.
Compare a windless day where nothing waves with a fan (moving air) making a still branch wave — notice the moving air moves the branch.
State in your own words what wind actually is and what is really happening with the trees.
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is moving air, and the moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees do not make the wind. Cause goes from moving air to moving object, not the reverse.

activities.title: Sort and order by what wind does
feedback: For sorting, link back to the scene: 'A leaf blows away in a breeze, but it takes a much stronger wind to move heavier things like a hat or branches — and a big heavy rock barely moves at all.'
If ordering is muddled, anchor on effects: 'Fluttering leaves is gentler than a bending tree.'
If a learner says you can SEE the wind, correct: 'We see what the wind does and the things it carries — not the moving air itself.'
activities.rationale: A sort/order/question check confirms the observational targets (define wind, breeze vs gale, examples of what wind moves). This sort and ordering can check classification and recall but does not itself build the felt breeze-to-gale spectrum; use it after hands-on and model experience.
learnerActions: Sort objects into 'the wind can move this easily' (kite, leaves, flag, hat, washing) versus 'the wind can't easily move this' (heavy rock).
Put effects in order from gentle to strong: leaves flutter → branches sway → hard to walk / tree bends.
Answer 'what is wind?' and explain how you know it's windy if you can't see the wind.
Tell a gentle breeze apart from a strong gale and give an example of each.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking that wind is moving air known by its effects, that some things move in wind and heavy things resist, and that strength runs along a spectrum from breeze to gale.

activities.title: How do you know it's windy? (talking it through)
feedback: Prompt for a second clue if a learner gives only one: 'That's one way — the flag is flapping. What else tells you it's windy?'
Praise effect-based answers: 'Yes — you feel it push and you see things move; both tell you the air is moving.'
activities.rationale: A brief eliciting conversation can draw out effects-based reasoning and give the learner practice producing an explanation, though a 5–7 observational concept does not require extended open dialogue.
learnerActions: Answer a prompt such as 'How do you KNOW it's windy if you can't see the wind? Give me two ways.'
Describe the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong gale in your own words.
Work out, with windows shut indoors, how you could make a little wind yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating that we detect wind only by its effects, and that strength varies, strengthens the observe-by-effects reasoning.

constraints: Keep the CAUSE of wind (uneven heating / rising air) out at this age — it is the later 7–9 'What Causes Wind' topic. Confine work to observing and describing.
Resist reversed cause ('wind is made by trees/fans/clouds waving') and animistic framing ('the weather is angry'); the moving air makes things move, not the reverse.
Build strength as a spectrum (breeze → wind → gale with matching effects) rather than a simple windy/not-windy split.
Clarify that windy does not always mean cold — wind can be warm or cold; strength and temperature are separate.

Lead with first-hand experience (blowing, fanning, a windy-day walk, flying a streamer) before any screen model; the responsive on-screen scene is a model of real wind, not a substitute for feeling it.
Sorting/quiz tasks check recognition and recall but do not themselves build the felt breeze-to-gale spectrum; use them after hands-on and model work, not instead of it.
Link to safety/daily life only gently (strong wind can knock things over, lifts kites) without drifting into separate storm-safety content.
Distinguish wind (moving air outdoors) from a fan or breath (moving air we make) — same idea, different source.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activities were reordered on review so the embodied 'Make your own wind' precedes the on-screen responsive scene, resolving a contradiction with the summary and constraint that first-hand experience come before any screen model.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the row (DfE KS1 detail and the misconception-research claim); the NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim establishes wind as a named weather condition (topic-level support) but does not directly support the specific teaching approach of any single activity, so it was not attached as an activity sourceClaim.

Interactive examples (wind-strength slider/dial, draggable objects, windsock angle, 'blow' button) are retained as optional ways to make the concept concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms; a tap-to-reveal windy scene is an acceptable lighter alternative for recap.

The non-preferred 3D option was rated 'poor' in the row with the note that observing wind by effects 'has no 3D requirement' — retained only as the catalog's narrow judgement for this concept, not as a universal claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.

No arithmetic or force-direction claims required correction here; the main conceptual safeguards are keeping the deferred cause-of-wind mechanism out and preserving the correct direction of cause (moving air moves objects).

probeDeeper: If we can't see the wind, how do we know it's there? Give me two ways.
What's the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong gale?
Indoors with the windows shut, could you make a little wind yourself? How?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it's the other way round. Wind is moving air. The moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave; the trees aren't making the wind. We can't see the air itself, but we can see what it does.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversed causality — 'trees (or waves, or leaves) make the wind by moving'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flip the cause: show a windless day where nothing waves, then a fan (moving air) making a still branch wave — the air moves the object.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the trees make the wind by waving their branches.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the moving object as the cause of the wind rather than its effect

errorPatterns.pattern: Wind isn't air — 'it's a special thing on its own'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make air tangible: fan the child's face, wave a hand, blow — that felt push is moving air, which is all wind is.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wind isn't air — it's a special thing on its own.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that wind is simply air that is moving

errorPatterns.pattern: Wind issues from a fixed source — 'it comes out of the sky'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show wind can come from any direction and that we make it by moving air ourselves, so it isn't from a single source.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Locates wind as pouring from one place rather than air moving from place to place

responseLevels.gap: Says the trees (or waves) make the wind; treats wind as not-air or as coming from a source.
responseLevels.full: States wind is moving air that pushes the branches (not the reverse), knows we detect it by what it moves, distinguishes breeze from gale, and can make wind by moving air.
responseLevels.partial: Says wind is moving air but hesitates on the direction of cause, or can't connect that we detect it only by its effects.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a windy day, the branches of a tree are waving about. A child says, 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Is that right? What is the wind actually, and what's really happening with the trees?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands wind as moving air says the air moves the branches. A child with the reversed-causality idea says the trees make the wind — a documented young misconception — giving the opposite direction of cause.
